newsitem.title: PERU: Japan's Hashimoto to visit Peru in wake of crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto to visit Peru in wake of crisis.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will visit Peru this week to hear firsthand how troops stormed Tokyo's diplomatic residence to end a four-month hostage crisis, President Alberto Fujimori said on Monday.
Fujimori said Hashimoto would arrive on Friday and begin official activities the following day.

"The programme is being drawn up. We hope it is one that reaffirms the friendship between Peru and Japan," Fujimori told reporters during a visit to the military hospital where injured hostages and troops who rescued them were being treated.
"Of course the Peruvian government and I as president are going to receive him with the cordiality that Prime Minister Hashimoto deserves," Fujimori added.

Marxist rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 during a lavish reception held to celebrate the birthday of Japanese Emperor Akihito. They initially held more than 500 people captive but freed all except 72 key hostages.

Peru's traditionally strong relations with Japan -- one of its main aid donors -- were strained severely during the 126- day hostage saga, but have been solidified again since the conclusion of the crisis on April 22.
After the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) seized the Japanese ambassador's home, Tokyo repeatedly warned Peru against opting for a military solution.

Fujimori did not warn Hashimoto before the military operation that killed the 14 Tupac Amaru rebels, freed all but one of their captives, but also left one hostage and two soldiers dead. He said the element of surprise was paramount.
Despite being kept in the dark, Hashimoto was lavish in his praise of Fujimori's decision and sent his Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda to Lima in the days after to express his thanks.
This week's visit is intended to reiterate that thanks and further cement relations between Tokyo and the administration of Fujimori, himself the son of Japanese immigrants.
Fujimori said all the hostages and troops wounded in the rescue operation were recovering satisfactorily.
"Happily, they are all safe," he said.

Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, hit by a bullet in the leg, will be released from the hospital within a few days and carry out his official duties in a wheelchair, Fujimori said. Supreme Court judge Luis Serpa was recovering from a colon operation, while a relative of the president, Pedro Aritomi, needed a muscle graft.
"Among the commandos, one suffered the amputation of a foot, another is recovering his vision, another commando has splinters in his shoulder and one was taken to the United States," Fujimori said.
